brief.realWorld: Companies like Waymo and Tesla are already testing self-driving cars on real roads today.
brief.funFact: Some self-driving cars have driven millions of miles without a human touching the wheel!

lessons.title: Could Humans Live on Mars?
lessons.summary: Have you ever looked up at the sky and wondered what life would be like on Mars? Known as the 'Red Planet,' Mars is one of the most Earth-like planets in our solar system — but could we actually live there?
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Have you ever looked up at the sky and wondered what life would be like on Mars? Known as the 'Red Planet,' Mars is one of the most Earth-like planets in our solar system — but could we actually live there?

brief.realWorld: Space agencies like NASA and companies like SpaceX are actively developing plans to send humans to Mars within the next few decades. Technologies being invented for Mars — like water recycling and compact solar power — are also being used to help people on Earth!
brief.funFact: A day on Mars is only slightly longer than a day on Earth — about 24 hours and 37 minutes. So Martian colonists wouldn't have to adjust their sleep schedules too much!

lessons.title: How Do Your Eyes See Color?
lessons.summary: Have you ever wondered how you can see a green apple or a bright red cherry? The answer comes down to light, special cells in your eyes, and your incredible brain!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Have you ever wondered how you can see a green apple or a bright red cherry? The answer comes down to light, special cells in your eyes, and your incredible brain!

brief.realWorld: People who are colorblind have cones that work differently, making it hard to tell certain colors apart — most commonly red and green. Knowing this, designers make sure important signs and signals aren't based on color alone.
brief.funFact: Mantis shrimp have 16 types of color receptors compared to our 3 — making them one of the most color-sensitive creatures on Earth!

lessons.title: How Do Planes Fly?
lessons.summary: Have you ever looked up at a massive airplane and wondered how such a heavy machine stays in the air? The answer is all about science and engineering!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Have you ever looked up at a massive airplane and wondered how such a heavy machine stays in the air? The answer is all about science and engineering!

brief.realWorld: Every time you board a plane, you're experiencing centuries of physics and engineering at work. The same principles of lift and drag that make planes fly also apply to birds, kites, and even race cars (which use wings to push DOWN for better grip!).
brief.funFact: The wings of a large airplane like a Boeing 747 can flex up to 6 feet up and down during flight — this flexibility actually makes them stronger, not weaker!

lessons.title: What Is a Black Hole?
lessons.summary: Black holes are some of the most mysterious objects in space — places where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Black holes are some of the most mysterious objects in space — places where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape!

brief.realWorld: The supermassive black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy is called Sagittarius A*. Even though it's 26,000 light-years away, scientists can track stars orbiting it to study its massive gravitational pull.
brief.funFact: If you could somehow fall into a black hole, time would pass slower for you than for someone watching from far away — a real phenomenon called time dilation predicted by Einstein!

lessons.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
lessons.summary: When you look up at the sky, have you ever wondered why it's blue? The answer lies in sunlight and the tiny particles in our atmosphere!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: When you look up at the sky, have you ever wondered why it's blue? The answer lies in sunlight and the tiny particles in our atmosphere!

brief.realWorld: Next time you watch a sunset, you're actually seeing physics in action! The gorgeous reds and oranges are what's left after all the blue light has been scattered away by the atmosphere.
brief.funFact: On Mars, the sky appears pinkish-red because the dust particles in its thin atmosphere scatter red light instead of blue!

lessons.title: What Happens When You Sleep?
lessons.summary: When you sleep, it may feel like you're doing nothing — but your brain and body are actually super busy! Sleep is one of the most important functions of your body.
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: When you sleep, it may feel like you're doing nothing — but your brain and body are actually super busy! Sleep is one of the most important functions of your body.

brief.realWorld: Ever notice how you feel sharper and happier after a good night's sleep before a big exam? That's because your brain was busy consolidating everything you studied while you were dreaming!
brief.funFact: During REM sleep, your body actually temporarily paralyzes your muscles so you don't act out your dreams — your brain is that active!

lessons.title: How Does the Internet Work?
lessons.summary: When you watch YouTube, play games, or message friends, it's all thanks to the internet — a massive connected computer system spanning the entire world. But how does it actually work?
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: When you watch YouTube, play games, or message friends, it's all thanks to the internet — a massive connected computer system spanning the entire world. But how does it actually work?

brief.realWorld: Every time you stream a Netflix show, the video is broken into thousands of tiny packets that travel through undersea cables and dozens of servers before reassembling on your screen — all in less than a second!
brief.funFact: There are over 400 undersea internet cables stretching more than 1.2 million kilometers across the ocean floor, carrying about 95% of all international internet traffic!

lessons.title: Hydropower: How Does It Work?
lessons.summary: Hydropower produces almost 20% of the world's energy! Discover how rushing water gets turned into electricity that powers our homes, schools, and smartphones.
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Hydropower produces almost 20% of the world's energy! Discover how rushing water gets turned into electricity that powers our homes, schools, and smartphones.

brief.realWorld: The next time you flip on a light switch, there's a good chance the electricity came from a hydropower plant! Major rivers across the world — like the Colorado and Columbia Rivers in the U.S. — have large dams that generate electricity for millions of homes every day.
brief.funFact: The Hoover Dam on the Nevada-Arizona border can generate enough electricity to power over 1.3 million homes — all from the rushing power of the Colorado River!

lessons.title: The Amazing Power of the Atom ⚡
lessons.summary: The word 'nuclear' sounds massive, but it actually describes something tiny — atoms! Scientists have found a way to unlock the incredible energy hiding inside them to power our entire world.
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: The word 'nuclear' sounds massive, but it actually describes something tiny — atoms! Scientists have found a way to unlock the incredible energy hiding inside them to power our entire world.

brief.realWorld: About 20% of the electricity in the United States comes from nuclear power plants. Countries like France generate over 70% of their electricity from nuclear energy. It's one of the largest sources of clean energy on the planet.
brief.funFact: A single uranium fuel pellet — about the size of a pencil eraser — contains as much energy as 17,000 cubic feet of natural gas, 1,780 pounds of coal, or 149 gallons of oil!

lessons.title: Why Is the Statue of Liberty Green?
lessons.summary: Lady Liberty wasn't always green — she used to look like a shiny new penny! The science behind her color change is more fascinating than you'd think.
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Lady Liberty wasn't always green — she used to look like a shiny new penny! The science behind her color change is more fascinating than you'd think.

brief.realWorld: Oxidation and patina formation happen on copper roofs, old coins, and outdoor sculptures all over the world. The same science that turned the Statue of Liberty green protects copper pipes in buildings and is used in chemistry and engineering every day.
brief.funFact: The Statue of Liberty is covered in about 80 tons of copper — roughly the same weight as 10 elephants — and it took around 20-30 years for the copper to fully turn green after it was unveiled in 1886!

lessons.title: Solar Power: How We're Catching the Sun's Energy
lessons.summary: The Sun sends more energy to Earth in one hour than every human uses in an entire year — and we've figured out how to catch it. Here's how solar power is changing the world!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: The Sun sends more energy to Earth in one hour than every human uses in an entire year — and we've figured out how to catch it. Here's how solar power is changing the world!

brief.realWorld: Babcock Ranch in Florida is America's first fully solar-powered town. Companies like Apple, Google, and NASA already run on solar energy. Solar panels can be found on rooftops, in space, and even on small everyday devices like calculators.
brief.funFact: The Sun delivers more energy to Earth in just ONE hour than all of humanity uses in an entire year — and solar panels let us tap into that incredible power!

lessons.title: How Bionic Limbs Are Changing Lives
lessons.summary: Almost 5,000 children lose their limbs every year — but thanks to bionic technology, many are able to live completely normal lives. Find out how!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Almost 5,000 children lose their limbs every year — but thanks to bionic technology, many are able to live completely normal lives. Find out how!

brief.realWorld: Bionic and prosthetic limbs are used by thousands of people around the world today, from Paralympic athletes to kids who just want to play with their friends. Companies like Open Bionics make the Hero Arm — a real, affordable bionic arm that kids can actually use.
brief.funFact: Jeremy Campbell won a gold medal in discus throwing at the Paralympics — using a prosthetic leg! Advanced footwork is key to throwing a discus, and his prosthetic made it possible.

lessons.title: Why Does Ice Float?
lessons.summary: Discover the surprising science behind why ice floats instead of sinking - and why this matters for life on Earth!
lessons.subject: 5 Minutes of STEM
objectives: Discover the surprising science behind why ice floats instead of sinking - and why this matters for life on Earth!

brief.realWorld: This property of water is essential for life! Fish, frogs, and other aquatic creatures survive frozen winters because ice forms a protective layer on top of lakes and ponds, while the water below stays liquid.
brief.funFact: About 90% of an iceberg is hidden underwater - that's where the phrase 'tip of the iceberg' comes from! The Titanic hit an iceberg in 1912 because the crew couldn't see how massive it really was below the surface.

labEquipment.name: Beaker Set
labEquipment.description: Graduated beakers let scientists measure and mix liquids precisely. Every real lab starts here.

labEquipment.name: Magnifying Glass
labEquipment.description: A convex lens that bends light to enlarge small details, used by naturalists for centuries.

labEquipment.name: Digital Thermometer
labEquipment.description: Measures temperature by sensing how materials change with heat. Essential for chemistry and biology.

labEquipment.name: Precision Scale
labEquipment.description: Accurate to a tenth of a gram. Careful measurement is what separates an experiment from a guess.

labEquipment.name: Bunsen Burner
labEquipment.description: The classic lab heat source, invented in 1855. Controlled flames enable reactions and sterilization.

labEquipment.name: Plant Growth Station
labEquipment.description: Grow lights and trays for botany experiments. Track how light, water, and soil change plant growth.

labEquipment.name: Electromagnet Kit
labEquipment.description: Coils, cores, and compasses for exploring the invisible force fields that power motors and generators.

labEquipment.name: Compound Microscope
labEquipment.description: Stacks two lenses to magnify up to 1000x, revealing cells, microbes, and crystal structures.

labEquipment.name: Circuit Workbench
labEquipment.description: Breadboards, LEDs, and resistors for building real electronics without soldering.

labEquipment.name: Chemistry Fume Hood
labEquipment.description: Ventilated workspace that safely carries fumes away. Safety equipment makes bolder experiments possible.

labEquipment.name: Refractor Telescope
labEquipment.description: Gathers far more light than your eye, bringing the Moon's craters and Jupiter's moons into view.

labEquipment.name: Ecosystem Aquarium
labEquipment.description: A self-contained water ecosystem for studying food webs, nitrogen cycles, and animal behavior.

labEquipment.name: Weather Station
labEquipment.description: Barometer, anemometer, and rain gauge. Meteorologists use these instruments to forecast storms.

labEquipment.name: Robotic Arm
labEquipment.description: Programmable servos and joints, like the robots that assemble cars and explore Mars.

labEquipment.name: 3D Printer
labEquipment.description: Builds objects layer by layer from melted plastic. Engineers prototype ideas overnight with these.

labEquipment.name: Laser Optics Bench
labEquipment.description: Mirrors, prisms, and beam splitters for exploring how light reflects, refracts, and interferes.

labEquipment.name: DNA Sequencer
labEquipment.description: Reads the genetic code letter by letter. Sequencing the first human genome took 13 years; now it takes hours.

labEquipment.name: Wind Tunnel
labEquipment.description: Blows controlled air over models to test aerodynamics, just like NASA and race car designers.

labEquipment.name: Spectrometer
labEquipment.description: Splits light into its spectrum to identify what things are made of, even distant stars.

labEquipment.name: Supercomputer Cluster
labEquipment.description: Thousands of processors working together to simulate weather, molecules, and galaxies.

labEquipment.name: Electron Microscope
labEquipment.description: Uses electron beams instead of light to see objects a million times smaller than a millimeter.

labEquipment.name: Tesla Coil
labEquipment.description: A resonant transformer that hurls artificial lightning. Nikola Tesla built the first one in 1891.

labEquipment.name: Clean Room Module
labEquipment.description: An ultra-filtered room with almost zero dust, where microchips and spacecraft parts are assembled.

labEquipment.name: Planetarium Dome
labEquipment.description: A projection dome that recreates the night sky from anywhere on Earth, at any point in history.
